title: Find lines of symmetry in shapes and designs

lesson.title: Folding Shapes in Half: Lines of Symmetry

steps.say: You already know a rectangle is a polygon with four straight sides. Today we learn one small idea: how to find the fold lines, called lines of symmetry, that cut a shape into two matching halves.

visual.caption: A rectangle, 8 cm long and 4 cm wide

steps.say: Here is the test. Imagine the shape is a piece of paper. If you fold it on a line and the two halves land exactly on top of each other, with no bits sticking out, that fold line is a line of symmetry. Think of folding a sandwich so the two pieces match perfectly.

visual.caption: Fold it and check: do the halves match exactly?

steps.say: Let's try it on this 8 centimetre by 4 centimetre rectangle. Fold it straight up and down through the middle. The left half is 4 centimetres wide and the right half is 4 centimetres wide, and both are 4 centimetres tall. They match perfectly, so that is one line of symmetry. Now fold it side to side through the middle. The top half is 8 centimetres by 2 centimetres and the bottom half is 8 centimetres by 2 centimetres. They match too. So a rectangle has two lines of symmetry.

visual.caption: Two folds work: up-and-down and side-to-side

steps.say: Now the tricky part that fools lots of kids. Many people say a rectangle has four lines of symmetry, because they also count the two corner-to-corner slanted lines, called diagonals. Let's check with the fold test. Fold the 8 by 4 rectangle along a diagonal. One half is a long skinny triangle with a side of 8 centimetres lying on top of a side of only 4 centimetres. Big corners poke out past the edge. The halves do not match, so a diagonal is not a line of symmetry.

visual.caption: Folding on the diagonal leaves this long triangle sticking out

steps.say: So a rectangle has exactly two lines of symmetry, not four. And here is something neat: a square is special, because its four sides are all the same length, so its diagonals do fold perfectly. But a rectangle that is longer than it is wide never works that way.

visual.caption: A 5 cm square is the special case where diagonals do match

steps.say: Remember: don't count a line just because it looks fair. Fold it in your mind and check that the two halves land exactly on top of each other.

lesson.answer: A line of symmetry is a fold line where both halves match exactly — a rectangle has 2, and its diagonals do not count.

practice.question: Ms. Yuanyuan's classroom door is a rectangle, 200 centimetres tall and 80 centimetres wide. Draw it on paper. How many lines of symmetry does the door have, and where are they?
practice.answer: Two. One goes straight down the middle from top to bottom, making two halves that are each 200 centimetres tall and 40 centimetres wide. The other goes straight across the middle, making two halves that are each 100 centimetres tall and 80 centimetres wide. The corner-to-corner diagonals are not lines of symmetry, because 200 centimetres and 80 centimetres are not the same, so the halves would not match.
